title: Latin in the Valley of Dry Bones
author: Luke Patient
summary: Luke Patient, a former master Latin teacher at Great Hearts, argues that classical schools should openly embrace Latin as a dead language rather than rebranding it as 'Living Latin.' He explains the slogan's appeal: Latin teachers constantly face the 'dead language' charge as a threat to their programs and their sense of purpose, and new spoken, active, and comprehensible-input methods arrive wrapped in the authority of second language acquisition research. Patient grants that these methods have a genuine strength in restoring active production, but contends that denying Latin's deadness quietly concedes the utilitarian premise that relevance is the measure of educational value, a premise that also turns History into Social Studies and Humane Letters into ELA. Pedagogically, he warns that treating Latin like a modern language produces an artificial 'Neo-Latin' that dresses contemporary concepts in Latin while authentic texts recede from view. His resolution is to distinguish intermediate objects, such as novellas and TPR exercises, from the proper object of study, authentic classical texts, insisting that the true end of Latin is contact with the wisdom of the past.
points: Patient argues 'Living Latin' is psychologically attractive because it seems to defeat the 'dead language' accusation that threatens programs and teachers' sense of meaning.
Denying Latin's deadness leaves intact the utilitarian premise that relevance determines value, the same premise that reshapes history, arts, and humane letters into more 'useful' subjects.
Spoken and comprehensible-input methods are credited with restoring active linguistic production, a practice with roots in late antique and medieval teaching.
When conversational 'Neo-Latin' becomes the goal, students receive the modern world 'with a coat of Latin spray-paint' rather than the world of Horace, Vergil, and Cicero.
Active methods are legitimate as intermediate objects only insofar as they remove barriers and lead students toward authentic Latin texts, the proper object of study.
quotes: But the opinion that Latin is a living language, whether harbored among the professed ignorati or the honorary illuminati, is wrong. The Latin that classical educational programs aim to teach is dead, and no amount of wishful thinking or persuasion can bring it back to life.

Living Latin,” as a slogan, appeals strongly to the embattled psyche of the practicing Latin teacher, for whom the sentence, “Latin is a dead language” is now most often encountered as a challenge. From the earliest days of mass public education in the United States, Latin has been under constant pressure from advocates of more “relevant” or “useful” elective modern languages. As the case now stands, the accusation of “deadness” often seems to students, parents, and administrators alike, a sufficient argument to justify the exclusion of Latin from the curriculum.

Whatever judgment we finally render upon G-T, the new pedagogies, with slogans such as “Spoken Latin,” “Active Latin,” or “Living Latin,” possess one truly outstanding strength: they restore active linguistic production as both a method and a symptom of genuine linguistic mastery. In so doing, the more historically conscious of them recover traditional techniques employed from late antiquity through the Middle Ages and beyond.

The psychological appeal—who wouldn’t prefer the living to the “dead”?—is a tacit affirmation of relevance and usefulness as the criteria of value. Education must be “relevant”, is the assumption; old and dead things aren’t relevant; therefore, Latin shouldn’t be a part of education. If we deny that Latin is dead, this argument fails to land. But by evading the conclusion in this way, we allow the premise about relevance to stand and even seem to approve it.

A dead language is certainly not “relevant” in the same way that a living one is, but relevance (and utility) is not the only kind of value that education can offer. Relevance, as utility, is a transitory type of value: what is useful today may become useless tomorrow; what is relevant changes constantly. Classical education is committed to the pursuit of, not transitory, but transcendent value for our students, directing them towards Truth, Goodness, and Beauty and (as is often done) referring to these as transcendentals.

The demand for utility silently presses the other disciplines towards the point of transmutation. Through relevance, History becomes Social Studies, the Fine Arts become electives, Humane Letters become ELA, and the sciences (once known as natural philosophy) lose their investigative impetus and become repositories of useful facts.

A Neo-Latin novella, a TPR exercise, or an active conversation may serve as an intermediate object, just as a textbook does. Any such object may be employed as a means provided it conduces toward the proper object of study. Its legitimacy is instrumental; it should remove barriers, cultivate facility, and prepare students to enter authentic Latin texts.
